# Maximising the potential of the National Compulsory Service Programme in rural China: a mixed methods study

**Authors:** Hange Li; Xidong Guo; Ziting Guo; Peicheng Wang; Yanhua Chen; Lijun Shen; Xuejun Zeng; Yanrong He; Yanrong Du; Wannian Liang; Jiming Zhu

**Affiliations:** 1Vanke School of Public Health, Tsinghua University, Beijing, China | 2Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 3Institute for Healthy China, Tsinghua University, Beijing, China | 4Department of Family Medicine and Division of General Internal Medicine, Peking Union Medical College Hospital, Beijing, China | 5General Practice School, Southern University of Science and Technology, Shenzhen, Guangdong, China

## Abstract

To alleviate the shortage of qualified physicians in rural areas, since 2010, the Chinese government has launched a National Compulsory Service Programme (NCSP) to enrol medical students for future work in township health centres (THCs) as general practitioners (GPs). The educational background of NCSP GPs is the best at THCs. This study aims to evaluate whether NCSP GPs have contributed to improving the quality of patient care at THCs and in what way.

This is an explanatory sequential mixed methods study.

NCSP GPs are assigned to THCs in the rural areas of central and western China, where assistant physicians are permitted to practice independently as licensed physicians. The contribution of NCSP GPs was defined as the extent to which they were perceived to improve the quality of care at THCs. Job performance was defined as the aggregated value to the organisation of discrete behaviour episodes that an individual performs.

For the quantitative component, nine provinces were selected by using a stratified random sampling method based on NCSP admission numbers. A total of 2815 THC leaders completed the survey (response rate, 32%). For the qualitative component, 33 NCSP GPs were recruited for semi-structured interviews through purposive and snowball sampling method.

The contribution of NCSP GPs to improvements in the quality of care at THCs was assessed as a key outcome measure.

68% of THC leaders reported that NCSP GPs contributed considerably to improving the quality of care. The contribution of NCSP GPs was significantly and positively associated with the performance of NCSP GPs themselves (β=0.789, 95% CI 0.724 ~ 0.854) and THC remoteness (β=0.144, 95% CI 0.067 ~ 0.222), but negatively associated with the percentage of licensed physicians at the THC (β=−0.340, 95% CI −0.483 ~ −0.197) and with the turnover of NCSP GPs (β=−0.119, 95% CI −0.221 ~ −0.016). The percentage of licensed physicians has a mediating role between THC remoteness and the contribution of NCSP GPs. Interviews revealed that NCSP GPs contributed to the THC as individual clinicians, and a majority also contributed by influencing others or participating in THC management, such as by improving diagnosis and treatment performance of others, standardising patient care, teaching and training and implementing safety processes.

NCSP GPs have a positive impact on the quality of care at THCs. In addition to working as individual competent physicians, they can contribute to the THCs in many ways. Adjustments in NCSP curriculum design, more supportive measures and better allocation processes are recommended to maximise this programme’s potential.

Keywords: Primary Health Care, Health Workforce, Quality in health care, Human resource management, China

- A mixed-methods evaluation in multiple provinces.

- We enrolled 1942 township health centres (THCs) for the qualitative part, and 33 interviewees for the qualitative part.

- The mechanisms of how the percentage of licensed physicians impacts the contribution of the National Compulsory Service Programme (NCSP) general practitioners (GPs) were explained by the qualitative part.

- This is a cross-sectional study, and the response rate of THCs was 32%, which is relatively low.

- The contribution of NCSP GPs to improving patient care at THCs is a subjective evaluation.

## Introduction

Human resources for health are fundamental to building and operating health systems.1 2 In WHO’s Operational Framework for Primary Health Care, the workforce was listed as one of the vital operational levers for a sustainable primary healthcare system.3 In addition to the accessibility of health resources and financial protection, delivering quality health services is essential to universal health coverage and investing in the workforce is critical.4 Qualified staff are the necessary prerequisite to the continuous quality improvement of primary healthcare service.5 6

China, as a large country covering 9.6 million square kilometres and with a population of more than 1.4 billion, has always struggled to develop adequate healthcare for rural populations. Shortly after the founding of the People’s Republic of China in 1949, a three-tiered health system composed of county hospitals (one for each county), township health centres (THCs, one for each township) and village clinics (at least one for each village) was rapidly established in rural China (figure 1).7 The barefoot doctor policy was implemented nationwide in the 1960s as an efficient approach to developing a rural workforce. Most barefoot doctors at village clinics only completed secondary school education and received 3–6 months of training in a hospital.8 With only this level of education and experience, they were not as well prepared as fully qualified doctors.9 In 1985, in order to improve the quality of rural doctors, the Ministry of Health abolished the barefoot doctor policy. In the same year, only half of the barefoot doctors passed a certification examination and became village doctors. The eligibility requirements and the difficulty level of the certification examination are much lower than those of the medical licensing examination.10

Prioritising the quantity of physicians at the expense of their quality also exists at THCs. Typically, a THC has 10–20 physicians and a total of 40 staff to provide essential medical and public health services to a rural population.11 Today, the Law of the People’s Republic of China on Medical Practitioners still permits assistant physicians who graduated from technical secondary school or junior college to practice independently in village clinics and/or THCs.12 The assistant physicians are also allowed to take the Chinese Medical Licensing Examination and become licensed physicians after a few years’ practice. As a result, in the whole nation, 39% of the physicians at THCs are assistant physicians and 58.2% of the licensed physicians in THCs do not have a bachelor’s degree. These rates are even higher in more rural areas.13

To alleviate the shortage of qualified physicians in THCs and to increase general practitioners (GPs) in primary care service, in the year of 2010, the Chinese government launched a National Compulsory Service Programme (NCSP) to develop medical students for service in THCs in central and western provinces.14 The students were enrolled via the National College Entrance Examination, and their tuition fees for the 5-year medical college education were waived. In return, they were committed to providing compulsory service as GPs in designated THCs for 6 years.15 In 2013, in a new training requirement, standardised residency training was implemented.16 Under this new policy, the NCSP was adjusted to 5-year medical college education, 3-year standardised residency training at tertiary hospitals and 3-year THC service.17 The combination of 5-year college education and 3-year residency training makes NCSP GPs the best-educated physicians likely to serve at THCs.

According to WHO, almost all the countries have difficulties in adequate qualified healthcare workforce in rural areas, and more than 70 countries have or had NCSP.18 China’s NCSP is unique in providing better educated physicians than the original physicians in rural areas. To date, approximately 80 000 students in total have been admitted to medical schools under NCSP in China, and nearly 20 000 of them work at THCs. While the enrolment, curriculum and retention rate of this programme is well documented, there is a dearth of literature regarding how NCSP GPs impact THCs and their special contributions as the best-educated physicians in rural areas.19,22 The present study aimed to evaluate whether NCSP GPs have contributed to promoting the quality of patient care at THCs and in what way. We believe the experience and lessons from China will be informative to other countries, especially to low- and middle-income countries.

## Methods

Ethical approval was granted by the institutional review board. An explanatory sequential mixed methods design was employed. The quantitative component (a survey) was conducted between December 2021 and February 2022, and the qualitative component (semi-structured interviews) was conducted between November 2022 and March 2023. Informed consent was obtained before the survey and before each interview.

### Definition of terms

We used the definition of ‘quality of care’ provided by the Institute of Medicine: ‘the degree to which health care services for individuals and populations increase the likelihood of desired health outcomes and are consistent with current professional knowledge’.23 The framework for ‘quality of care’ used in this study was adopted from the Quality Framework for Australian General Practice, which includes the dimensions of acceptability, accessibility, appropriateness, effectiveness, efficiency and safety.24 Contribution was defined as the extent to which NCSP GPs were perceived to improve the quality of care at THCs. Job performance was defined as the ‘aggregated value to the organization of discrete behaviour episodes that an individual performs’.25

### Quantitative component: participants, procedures and data analysis

The questionnaire was designed for the THC leaders to complete. By using a stratified random sampling method based on NCSP admission numbers, 9 provinces or autonomous regions were selected from 22 that had implemented the programme, namely Shanxi, Jilin, Anhui, Hubei, Guangxi, Hainan, Guizhou, Qinghai and Xinjiang (online supplemental appendix 1). The details of the sampling process were previously published.26 To develop the questionnaire, we first conducted a literature review and several interviews with THC leaders. We then drafted the questionnaire and collected feedback through two rounds of expert discussions. A pilot study was conducted in 12 THCs, after which some final adjustments were made. The final questionnaire (online supplemental appendix 2) collected the following information about each THC: (1) basic information such as name and address, (2) human resources, (3) the number of NCSP GPs, (4) the evaluation of the NCSP GPs. The performance evaluation of NCSP GPs was subdivided into four aspects, namely work attitude, patient care ability, communication skills and adaptability skills in rural areas. Each rating was a response to a 5-point Likert scale (1=very unsatisfied, 5=very satisfied, 6=unable to evaluate). If there was more than one NCSP GP at a THC, the THC leader assessed the average performance of all NCSP GPs. Cronbach’s alpha of the four items in our sample was 0.95. The overall performance was calculated as the average score of the four performance evaluation aspects. The contribution of NCSP GPs to improving the quality of care at the THC was also rated on a 5-point Likert scale (1=almost none, 5=very much). To reduce social desirability bias, the respondents were assured that the questionnaire would not be used to evaluate their institution. The exclusion criteria were: (1) incomplete questionnaire, (2) the respondent’s position did not belong to THC leaders, (3) the respondent chose ‘unable to evaluate’ in any evaluation question.

THC remoteness was determined using the classification issued by the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security of the People’s Republic of China in 2006, based on both the natural geographical environment and socioeconomic development.27 The indicators of the natural geographical environment included altitude, soil type, water resources, terrain ruggedness and the climate comfort index (which included factors such as temperature, wind speed and solar radiation). The indicators of socioeconomic development included the remoteness index (which included factors such as transportation and communication) and the human development index (which included public services such as education, healthcare and fiscal revenue).

The sample size calculated by PASS software identified that 1574 THCs were needed to achieve a 0.05 significance level. Considering a missing rate of 20%, at least 1889 THCs with NCSP GPs should be reached. The questionnaire was in electronic form and was sent by ‘Wenjuanxing’ (a widely used online survey tool in China) to the THC leaders with the support of the National Health Commission. Most questions in the electronic questionnaires were required questions.

Duplicate responses were removed based on the name of THCs. Descriptive analyses were used to report the average and proportional features. Multivariable linear regression analysis was conducted to investigate associations between potential factors (THC remoteness, number of physicians, percentage of licensed physician, number of NCSP GPs, turnover of NCSP GP and overall performance of NCSP GPs) and NCSP GPs’ contribution. The potential mediating roles of the number and percentage of licensed physicians at the THC in the relationship between THC remoteness and NCSP GPs’ contribution were also explored. Robust SEs were clustered at the county level. The statistical analyses were performed using Stata V.17.0.

### Qualitative component: participants, procedures and data analysis

A qualitative study may reveal the details and provide further understandings in how the NCSP GPs impact the THCs. The interview participants were NCSP GPs working in THCs. They were recruited by purposive and snowball sampling. The seed interviewees were successful NCSP GPs provided by the National Health Commission and other participants were referred by the seeds. All the participants were interviewed separately to preserve interviewee independence. The interviews lasted 18–45 min. Participants were offered ¥200 (about US$25) as compensation for their time. Recruitment ceased when data saturation was achieved.

The interview guide (online supplemental appendix 3) included several open-ended questions to encourage the participants to share what they did for the THCs. The main questions were: (1) What did you do for the THC as an NCSP GP? (2) What changes did you bring to your THC? (3) What impact have you had on the residents there? (4) What impact has the NCSP had on your life? (4) What do you think about the quality of healthcare at THCs compared with tertiary hospitals?

Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, all the interviews were conducted online via video (Tencent Meeting). Author HL, with both clinical and management experience, conducted or observed all interviews. All the interviews were audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim. Thematic analysis was used and conducted using NVivo V.12 software. Authors HL and ZG developed and refined the coding framework under the guidance of XZ, a senior consultant in general practice and a head of the department of family medicine in a tertiary hospital. The main themes were borrowed from the Four Stages of Contribution model of Korn Ferry Institute, which was derived from the research pioneered by former Harvard Business School professors Gene Dalton and Paul Thompson.28 Among the several well-developed career stage theories in the realm of human resources management, this contribution model, though not the most widely used career stage theory, focused on the interactions the individuals have with other employees and the organisation as well.29 30 After the codebook was finalised and a common coding style was agreed on, HL and ZG coded the transcripts independently. Their percent agreement was 97.5% and Cohen’s kappa coefficient was 0.70.

### Patient and public involvement

Patients and/or the public were not involved in the design, or conduct, or reporting or dissemination plans of this research.

### Qualitative component

The data saturation was achieved after 21 interviews, confirmed with 12 interviews. Among the 33 participants, 23 were male and 10 were female, with an average of 31.3 years old. They worked in 32 different THCs in eight provinces for 0–4 years. About half of the participants had administrative posts such as vice president of the THC and director of the department of general practice (online supplemental appendix 4).

## Discussion

The implementation of China’s NCSP reflects the commitment of the Chinese government to promote human resources for health in rural areas. This programme has been in operation for 13 years, and this is the first study to depict the contribution of NCSP GPs in the improvement of patient care at THCs in rural China. In several respects, the programme appears to have been a success. NCSP GPs are having a positive impact on the quality of care at THCs. In addition to working as competent physicians, they are contributing to the THCs in many ways and improving the THC’s system of care.

The quality of care at some THCs is in need of improvement.31 32 Other research revealed that relatively few patients were given appropriate diagnostic tests,33 and unnecessary antibiotics were widely prescribed at THCs.34 The hypertension control rate varied from 0% to 62.4%, indicating substantial room for improvement at certain THCs.35 Our findings are consistent with these studies, as our interviewees also mentioned the lack of quality control and routine safety processes. As a result, Chinese patients do not trust primary care facilities and prefer to obtain high-quality medical services from larger hospitals.36

A majority of THC leaders regard NCSP GPs as making a considerable contribution to improving patient care in their THCs. The interviews of NCSP GPs reveal how important they have been for some backward THCs, in much more detail than the quantitative survey data reveal. None of the interviewees we encountered were in the career stage of contributing dependently, even though some interviewees just started working at THC a few months ago. All of them contributed independently, and the majority of them also contributed through others or strategically. Fresh from the residency training in tertiary hospitals, NCSP GPs did not take the unsatisfactory condition of THCs for granted but made every effort to change it. In addition to being competent physicians, NCSP GPs were also teachers for less-qualified colleagues, advocates for standard treatment and safety cultures and managers for departments or the whole THC. Our data strongly suggest that qualified physicians can have a powerful effect on the improvement of patient care in remote areas, even in their early stage of career.

The contribution of NCSP GPs was associated with many factors. Unsurprisingly, the NCSP GP’s performance had a strong correlation with their contribution evaluation. Previous studies have also found that self-reported job performance was good among NCSP graduates,22 but our results are more reliable as the daily performance of NCSP GPs was rated by other people.37 The combination of 5-year medical college education and 3-year residency training at tertiary hospitals prepared the national NCSP GPs well to be competent in patient care at THCs. Furthermore, the NCSP GPs can contribute to THCs in several additional ways. Given their efforts in programme and centre administration, it may be that the NCSP curriculum should be upgraded with some additional leadership development courses and more training in systems thinking.

Retaining NCSP GPs at THCs is also vital, as the turnover of NCSP GPs statistically decreases the contribution evaluation score, indicating that the good effect of NCSP GPs may not be sustained after their departure. The retention rate of NCSP GPs after their contract expired was low, as shown by other research.38 39 The main reasons for turnover intention are limited opportunities for career development and low income, suggesting that retention incentives such as good salary and improved working conditions should be considered for this programme to reach its full potential.39 40

The allocation of NCSP GPs to THCs also deserves more attention.41 There are distinct disparities in the geographical distribution of health resource in China.42 When the Chinese government launched this programme in 2010, the goal was to provide one NCSP GP to every THC in central and western China. As the programme progressed, the government realised that equity, instead of equality, should be more emphasised. In 2019, the government recommended priority for the allocation of NCSP GPs to areas with more population and fewer GPs.43 However, based on our findings, the NCSP GPs contribute more if they were assigned to remote THCs, as remote THCs are prone to have a lower percentage of qualified physicians. The qualitative component of this study elucidates the mechanism underlying greater contribution of NCSP GPs in certain THCs, as they can train the staff there, standardise their daily practice and establish safety protocols at THCs based on their experience at tertiary hospitals. Most interviewees achieved the level of contributing to their THCs through other people, which triangulated with the partial mediating effect of the percentage of licensed physician at the THC.

It may be difficult for other countries to replicate Chinese models for rural care improvement, but all countries can learn from each other through an exchange of experience and expertise. Other countries may not have assistant physicians, but may have other forms of healthcare professionals that can prescribe independently in rural areas,44,46 or distinct heterogeneities in health resources of health between rural areas and urban areas.47 When we provide human resources for health to less developed areas, in addition to their quantity issues, the quality of original healthcare workers should be taken into consideration. When implemented appropriately, the educationally linked compulsory service programme could improve the quality of care in rural areas profoundly.

### Limitations

This study has some limitations. First, the response rate of THCs was 32%, at a relatively low level. The survey of primary care facilities was difficult as they were highly separated. Some provinces distributed the questionnaire through official announcements. Others sent the questionnaire via an online working group. In some provinces, the THCs are hard to be contacted by provincial administrations, and the questionnaire was transferred to cities, counties and townships level by level. Still, this is to our knowledge the largest survey of THCs in China. We compared the characteristics of our respondent THCs with the National Statistic Yearbook (online supplemental appendix 5), and it turns out that our sample is representative of THCs overall in the number of physicians and in the number of licensed physicians.

Second, the performance and contribution evaluation of NCSP GPs is a rough estimate. Objective measures such as diagnostic accuracy and treatment plan accuracy were not readily available and were therefore not used in this study. It would be ideal if we adopted validated indicators and measurement instruments in the questionnaire survey. However, there is a lack of globally comparable and locally validated metrics that can reflect critical dimensions of healthcare quality.48 49 In fact, even the efforts to develop measurable quantitative indicators of high quality healthcare in low-income and middle-income countries aroused controversy.50 On the other hand, even if we could precisely measure the improvement of healthcare quality at a certain THC, it would also be challenging to calculate how much of the improvement is due to NCSP GPs using health economics methods. Consequently, a straightforward question was developed to capture the answer we are interested in. Regarding the performance evaluation of NCSP GPs, the Entrustable Professional Activities for GPs in rural China have not been established.51 The scope of GP’s roles and responsibilities in China remains elusive.52 The development of standardised measurement tools will undoubtedly enhance future research endeavours within this domain.

Third, there are omitted variables. The educational background and major of THC leaders may influence their vision and their evaluation of NCSP GPs. The support of THC could also have a significant impact on the job performance of NCSP GPs.53 We did not comprehensively and empirically evaluate the quality of care at our surveyed THCs. This is the first study focusing on the NCSP implementation at the institutional level and further research should be designed to give a more comprehensive assessment.

Fourth, there is selection bias in the qualitative component of our programme evaluation. The interviewee seeds were nominated by the National Health Commission and may represent the most successful practitioners among NCSP GPs. The results of the questionnaire survey have already shown that NCSP GPs were favourably rated. The qualitative interview-based exploration then aimed to further investigate how they made their contributions. The research design adopted a purposive sampling strategy where an enriched sample of successful NCSP GPs was included. However, not all NCSP GPs may be as successful as those we interviewed. In our interviews, these interviewees mentioned that they knew that some other NCSP GPs had less chance to do clinical work or contribute as much to THC overall. Another study has established, for example, that some physicians at THCs sometimes are largely responsible for public health service tasks.54 A larger study of a random sample of NCSP GPs would be necessary to document their typical working responsibilities.

## Conclusion

In conclusion, NCSP GPs have a positive impact on the quality of care at THCs. In addition to working as competent physicians, they can contribute to the THCs in many ways and improve the performance of THCs systemically. This study is the first to explore the contribution of NCSP GPs to improving the quality of care at THCs in rural China. Further research would benefit from more rigorous measures of the quality of care and job performance. We recommend incorporating systems thinking and management courses into the NCSP curriculum to better prepare them for contributing through others and strategically at THCs. In addition, implementing stronger incentive and support policies could encourage NCSP GPs’ retention. Finally, allocating NCSP GPs based on the remoteness of the area and the percentage of licensed physicians at THCs may help maximise their potential impact.

# Anesthesiology and Perioperative Science

# Anesthesiology practices in China: an updated nationwide cross‑sectional survey

Changsheng Zhang1,2†, Yixun Lu1,2†, Jingwei Liu3, Hange Li4, Yuguang Huang5, Weidong Mi1,2*    and Chinese Anesthesiology Department Tracking Collaboration Group

Abstract Purpose  Understanding the current status of a discipline is crucial for its robust and progressive development. In 2018, the first nationwide survey of Chinese anesthesiology provided critical insights into workforce distribution, patient outcomes, infrastructure, and educational resources. Given the dynamic nature of the discipline and the rapidly changing healthcare landscape, a follow-up survey was deemed essential to capture the current status of Chinese anesthesiology. Methods  This second round cross-sectional nationwide census survey was conducted from February 1, 2022, to August 31, 2022. Participants comprised each hospital department providing anesthesia services across the 31 provinces of mainland China. Data analysis was performed from January 2023 to January 2024. The survey content remains consistent with inaugural study, including general information of the department, hospital level and scale, volume of the anesthesiology department, characteristics of anesthesiologists, and anesthetic caseloads. Data were collected and uploaded using face-to-face interview conducted by trained interviewers. Data quality was controlled by electronic questionnaire and continuous oversight by the investigation committee throughout the whole process. Results  The nationwide census survey, conducted among 11,505 hospital departments providing anesthesia services in China, identified a total workforce of 105,732 anesthesiologists. This represents a 14% increase in the number of anesthesiologists over the preceding five-year period. The national anesthesiologist-to-population ratio was calculated at 7.5 per 100,000 individuals, with regions boasting higher gross domestic product per capita exhibiting a higher density of anesthesiologists. Additionally, the survey documented 25,056 anesthesia nurses contributing to the anesthesia workforce. Analysis of anesthesiologists’ workload indicated a compound annual growth rate of 2.72% from 2018 to 2020. Notably, non-operating room anesthesia cases demonstrated a growth rate approximately 7% higher than that of operating room anesthesia cases, suggesting a discernible shift in clinical practice patterns. Conclusions  Chinese anesthesiology has experienced rapid growth, underscored by the substantial expansion in its workforce. Nevertheless, persistent challenges necessitate ongoing attention. The findings derived from this nationwide survey provide critical insights for guiding the discipline’s future development and informing evidence-based policy-making. Keywords  Anesthesiology, Nationwide survey, Health policy, Workforce, Workload

1  Introduction In recent years, guided by the Health China Action Plan (2019–2030), China’s healthcare system has experienced substantial advancements in medical technology, quality, and services [1]. Notably, China’s Healthcare Access Quality (HAQ) index reached 70.2 in 2019, reflecting an absolute increase of 35.2 points from 1990 to 2019. This trajectory positioned China’s HAQ index at a level comparable to the average for countries with a high-middle Socio-demographic Index [2]. Simultaneously, the progressive growth of the discipline of anesthesiology in China has been synchronized with that of developed countries, which are concerned about postoperative outcomes, infection control and patient satisfaction, expanded the scope of anesthesiology to include what is now known as "perioperative medicine" [3]. According to annual statistics released by the National Health Commission (NHC), the total number of surgeries performed in Chinese hospitals was 81.03 million in 2021, representing an annual increase of exceeding 10% [4]. To meet the needs of the rapid growth of the number of surgeries and the aging population for healthcare services, the robust and upward development of anesthesiology departments in China is of paramount importance. In 2018, the Chinese Anesthesiology Department Tracking Collaboration Group conducted the inaugural nationwide survey, providing a comprehensive overview of the anesthesiology discipline in China and highlighting significant challenges, including heavy caseloads, a workforce shortages, and suboptimal resource configuration [5]. Subsequently, significant governmental and professional efforts have been implemented to address these critical issues. These endeavors have improved disciplinary structure, defining the scope of anesthesia services, optimizing the required anesthesiologist-to-population ratio, and increasing enrollment in anesthesia residency programs [6]. The anesthesiology landscape has undoubtedly undergone significant transformations following years of development and the impactful influence of the COVID-19 pandemic. Considering these dynamic changes within Chinese anesthesiology, we propose conducting an updated nationwide cross-sectional survey to provide a more nuanced understanding of the discipline’s current state and its evolving challenges. Therefore, a second-round cross-sectional nationwide census survey was design and executed by the Chinese Society of Anesthesiology (CSA). The survey leveraged the established Chinese Anesthesiology Department Tracking Database (CADTD), a web-based data collection system established in the initial survey. The primary objectives of this study were to comprehensively reassess the current status of anesthesiology discipline in China and to conduct a comparative analysis against the findings of the inaugural survey.

2  Methods 2.1  Data source and study sample The nationwide survey was conducted between February 1 st, 2022, and August 31th, 2022, encompassing all institutions listed in the CADTD as well as other unlisted institutions providing anesthesia services in China. Respondents included department chiefs or other designated individuals, typically administrative secretaries, within the anesthesia departments.

2.2  Questionnaire design and questionnaire investigations The questionnaire was developed based on the data requirements of the CADTD and specifications from the National Centre for Anesthesia Medical Quality and Quality Control. A total of 35 items were included, encompassing hospital tier and size, departmental configuration, annual workload (2018–2020), and workforce demographics.  The English version is available in the Supplemental Material. Investigators, organized into teams as in the first survey, underwent comprehensive online training and successfully passed an examination prior to conducting investigations. To ensure data clarity and minimize potential biases, face-to-face interviews were conducted with department chiefs or designated personnel. Written consent was obtained before data collection, and data entry was performed synchronously by investigators. The questionnaire was administered electronically through a dedicated online platform.

2.3  Quality control Rigorous quality control measures were implemented throughout the survey process, including consistency, plausibility, and accuracy checks within the electronic questionnaire. Provincial and municipal data specialists were responsible for monitoring data rationality, with unqualified questionnaire results undergoing to review and re-investigation. Of the 15,669 institutions initially identified as eligible, 1,425  (9.1%) refuse to participate, 1,149 (7.3%) has no anesthesia department, 1,590 (10.1%) duplicated records, 11,505 were successfully surveyed, yielding a response rate of 73.4%. We implemented a rigorous data collection and validation protocol consisting of four stages. First, primary data collection was conducted through submissions of participating institutions. Second, automated logic checks were applied by the electronic data capture system, which flagged inconsistencies, outliers, and missing entries in real-time. Third, investigator follow-up was performed, during which our research team directly contacted each institution to clarify or complete missing or anomalous data points. This

Descriptive statistics were used to summarize continuous and categorical variables, with inferential analyses including t-tests, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), Mann–Whitney U tests, and χ2 tests as appropriate. Pearson correlation and ANOVA were used to assess relationships and differences, respectively. A significance level of P < 0.05 was applied.

3.1  Departments providing anesthesia services in Mainland China In August 2022, there were 11,505 hospital departments offering anesthesia services across 31 provinces, autonomous regions, and municipalities in China. Among these, 3,294 (28.63%) were affiliated with tier 3 hospitals, 6,706 (58.28%) with tier 2 hospitals, and 1,505 (13.09%) with tier 1 or lower hospitals. Furthermore, there were 475,816 surgeons, averaging 41.37 surgeons per hospital. Consistent with expectations, higher tiers hospitals exhibited larger numbers of beds and surgeons. 3.3  Scope of practice in departments providing anesthesia services In Chinese anesthesiology departments, the reported coverage rates of practice scope were as follows: clinical anesthesia (97.88%), chronic pain diagnosis and treatment (25.50%), anesthesia intensive care unit (12.22%), and surgical intensive care unit (5.98%). Moreover, the popularization rates of labor analgesia and painless gastroscopy among these departments were 68.26% and 69.24%, respectively. Notably, a trend towards broader practice scope within anesthesia departments was observed in higher-tier hospitals. For detailed coverage rates and popularization rates by hospital tier, please refer to Supplementary Table S1.

3.4  The quality, quantity, and regional distribution of Chinese anesthesiologists Among the 11,505 department chiefs surveyed, the male-to-female ratio stood at 3.27:1. A substantial majority (81.93%) were over 40  years of age, with 46.67% falling within the 40–49  years. The mean working experience of anesthesiologists-in-chief was 21.81 ± 8.77  years. Regarding educational attainment, 69.18% of the anesthesiologists-in-chief held a bachelor’s degree, while 9.98% and 3.96% possessed master’s and doctoral degrees, respectively. Furthermore, 90.35% of department chiefs with doctoral degrees and 66.58% of those with chief ranking worked in tier 3 hospitals. Significant variations in the distribution of rankings and educational backgrounds were observed across the three hospitals tiers (Table  S2). A positive correlation was observed between hospital tier and the educational attainment of anesthesiologists. Specifically, 91.00% of anesthesiologists in tier 3 hospitals possessed bachelor’s degrees or higher, contrasting sharply with only 19.08% in tier 1 hospitals. Furthermore, the proportion of anesthesiologists with senior professional titles decreased

significantly as the hospital level decreased. For instance, less than 15% of anesthesiologists in tier 1 hospitals held senior professional titles, compared to 19.5% in tier 2 and 28.13% in tier 3 hospitals. As of August 2022, China reported a total of 105,732 anesthesiologists and 25,056 anesthesia nurses. Notably, the distribution of anesthesiologists varied significantly by hospital tier, with 46.86% in tier 3, 34.30% in tier 2, and 3.54% in tier 1. Despite an overall increase of 14.03% in the total number of anesthesiologists compared to 2018 (n = 92,726), the operating room to anesthesiologist ratio remained below the national standard for anesthesia departments (1:2), standing at less than 1:1.5. Furthermore, the anesthesiologist-to-surgeon ratio was 1:4.5 in 2022, suggesting a slower growth rate in anesthesiologist number relative to surgeons. Regarding anesthesia nurses, 98.69% (11,354) of departments providing anesthesia services were equipped with anesthesia nurses. Of these, 42.07% had full-time anesthesia nurses, and 56.61% had part-time anesthesia nurses, primarily from operating room nurse pools (85.97%). Detailed figures for the number of anesthesiologists, anesthesia nurses, surgeons, and their related ratios can be found in Table S3 and Table S4. In this survey, an average of 7.5 full-time equivalent anesthesiologists per 100,000 population were reported in China, an increase of 0.76 compared to the 2019 investigation. Despite this overall growth, a significant geographical disparity in anesthesiologist distribution persists across China. The per capita anesthesiologist ratio ranged from the highest of 15.10 per 100,000 in Beijing to the lowest of 4.2 per 100,000 in Tibet. Further details on the distribution of anesthesiologists in China are presented in Fig. 1. 4  Discussion This survey is the second comprehensive investigation into the current landscape of anesthesiology in China based upon a similar study conducted in 2019. Data from 11,432 departments nationwide providing anesthesia services encompassed updated general information and current operational conditions. Key observations between 2019 and 2022 revealed a significant 14% increase in the anesthesiologist workforce, exceeding 100,000 practitioners. Concurrently, the number of departments offering anesthesia services remained stable. Furthermore, a consistent upward trend in the utilization of labor analgesia

and painless gastroscopy was observed. Despite these positive developments, the longstanding issues of inequitable distribution of both anesthesiology personnel and workload persist. The findings offer an objective assessment of recent advancements and persistent challenges within Chinese anesthesiology, providing crucial insights for future developmental strategies and policy formulation.

4.1  Number of physician anesthesia providers The Chinese anesthesiologist workforce has demonstrated continuous and steady growth in recent years. Compared to the 2019 survey, the total number of anesthesiologists in China increased by 13,006. The anesthesiologist-to-population ratio rose from 5.7 per 100,000 in 2014 to 6.7 in 2019, and further to 7.5 in 2022, aligning with annual development targets and the expectations outlined in No. 21 document (Notice on Issuing Opinions on Strengthening and Improving Anesthesia Medical Services) [5]. Based on historical trends, China is poised for a substantial expansion of its anesthesiologist workforce to over 140,000, achieving a ratio exceeding 10 anesthesiologists per 100,000 population by 2030. And we can also expect a gradual transformation from a country with a large number of anesthesiologists and heavy anesthesia caseload to a country with a strong anesthesiology discipline, as introduced by the CSA annual meeting in 2023 [6]. Despite the majority of Chinese provinces achieving an anesthesiologist-to-population ratio of 6 per 100,000, significant disparities persist across China. Thirteen provinces have met or surpassed the national average ratio, whereas eighteen provinces and municipalities fall below it. Super-metropolitan areas like Beijing and Shanghai exhibit ratios exceeding 10 per 100,000, approaching mid-to-high global levels. Consistent with previous findings, this study underscores a strong correlation between regional economic development indicators—including GDP per capita, annual per capita consumption expenditure, and annual per capita disposable income—and the anesthesiologist-to-population ratio. In brief, regions with superior economic development tend to attract and retain a greater number of anesthesiologists. Notably, while Tibet experienced a 33.76% increase in its anesthesiologist-to-population ratio between the two survey cycles (from 3.14 to 4.2 per 100,000), this figure remains significantly lower than in other Chinese provinces and municipalities, likely attributable to geographical and economic constraints. However, simply increasing the number of anesthesiologists in less developed regions is unlikely to substantially mitigate these severe geographic disparities. Further, the addition of anesthesiologists to underserved areas may not yield significant improvements in population healthcare if essential supporting systems, such as surgical departments and infrastructure, are underdeveloped or absent [7]. Therefore, comprehensive and multi-faceted support measures, including incentives for anesthesiologists to practice in remote western China, should be simultaneously implemented by health commissions and academic societies. In addition, the recent growth in China’s anesthesiologist workforce has been predominantly concentrated in tier 3 hospitals, with an increase exceeding 30%. In contrast, changes anesthesiologist numbers in tier 2 and tier 1 hospitals were less pronounced. This trend intensifies the inverted triangular distribution of anesthesiologists across hospital tiers. Moreover, significant disparities in educational background and physician ranking persist between hospital tiers, potentially stemming from the current residency training structure and policies. The majority of anesthesia resident training bases are situated in teaching hospitals, university-affiliated hospitals, or tier 3 institutions. Consequently, well-trained residents completing systematic training programs often prefer to commence their careers in higher-tier hospitals rather than in grassroots medical units [8], leading to a gradual exacerbation of the polarized allocation of highly trained, academically qualified anesthesiologists among different hospital tiers.

4.2  Expansion of the anesthesia workload The workload of Chinese anesthesiologists experienced substantial increases, rising by 7.48% from 2017 to 2018, and by 8.58% from 2018 to 2019. In 2020, primarily due to the pandemic sweeping, the workload remained relatively stable compared to 2019. With the robust growth

of anesthesiologist workforce, the per capita workload in tier 3 hospitals gradually decreased from 706.78 in 2018 to 622.07 in 2020. Notably, tier 3 hospitals observed negative growth in per capita anesthesiologist workload for the first time in 2019. These findings suggest that recent policies promoting anesthesiology development have yielded positive outcomes, with the increased number of anesthesia providers beginning to alleviate the heavy workload. Undoubtedly, it is anticipated that occupational burnout and stress among Chinese anesthesiologists will diminish in the near future, consequently leading to improved patient care and safety. It’s worth mentioning that the comfort care services, including labor analgesia and painless gastroscopy, have gained significant popularity within Chinese anesthesiology departments, which probably contributed the majority of the NORA cases [9]. Driven by the NHC initiatives promoting pain-free natural childbirth, the prevalence of labor analgesia has undergone dramatic expansion over the past 5 years, increasing from 27.5% in 2017 to 53.2% in 2020, and reaching 68.3% by 2022 [10].

4.3  Major improvements and existing problems of Chinese anesthesiology The second-round nationwide survey summarized the current status and characteristics of anesthesiology in China. Significant and satisfactory progress has been observed in the discipline, largely attributable to four consecutive preferential policies supporting anesthesiology implemented by the government and health commission between 2017 and 2020 [11]. The average annual increase of anesthesiologists in China was about 4,300, leading to an anesthesiologist-to-population ratio of 7.5 per 100,000 in 2022. Consequently, the current development of the anesthesiology in China is progressively aligning with the burgeoning demand for healthcare services. Furthermore, the scope of practice and the provision of comfort care services by anesthesia departments have expanded, enabling more patients to receive comfort analgesia services. Despite these advancements, several persistent challenges continue to plague the development of Chinese anesthesiology. Although we are already a country with the highest number of anesthesiologists, a significant shortage is projected to persist for the foreseeable future. And a big gap remains between China and other developed countries in the anesthesiologist-to-population ratio, with distribution of anesthesiologists concentrating in better economic regions. Remote and economically underdeveloped areas face a critical need for anesthesiologists. Furthermore, the distribution of workload exhibits an imbalance and inverted pattern. 4.4  Limitations First, the questionnaire content was revised in alignment with the Chinese Association of Anesthesiologists guidelines and the National Centre for Anesthesia Medical Quality and Quality Control’s specifications, resulting in minor modifications compared to the prior survey. Second, the hospital registry experienced continuous changes due to hospital establishment, closures, and the ongoing impact of the pandemic, potentially affecting survey accuracy. Third, despite robust quality control measures, information bias remains a challenge. Questionnaire items were designed to accommodate the majority of Chinese hospitals; however, hospitals with limited scale or specialized focuses may present significantly different anesthesia department configurations. Moreover, respondent attitudes and levels of cooperation could influence survey outcomes.

5  Conclusions This study provides a comprehensive overview of the current status and recent development of anesthesiology in China over the past five years. The discipline has experienced rapid growth, evidenced by the substantial expansion in its workforce. Nevertheless, persistent challenges, including insufficient anesthesiologist numbers, regional disparities in development, and imbalanced workload distribution, necessitate continued strategic interventions. The findings of this survey offer critical insights to guide future disciplinary development and inform evidence-based policy-making.

Policy perception, job satisfaction and intentions to remain in rural area: evidence from the National Compulsory Service Programme in China

Yanrong He1†, Peicheng Wang1,2†, Yanrong Du1, Hange Li1, Yanhua Chen1,2* and Jiming Zhu1,3*

Abstract Background  Exploring factors that may influence general practitioners (GPs)’ intentions to remain in rural area is necessary to inform the training and placement of future medical workforce in rural area. However, little is known about how GPs’ perception towards the National Compulsory Service Programme (NCSP) and job satisfaction impact their turnover intention. This paper explores GPs’ intentions to remain in rural China and how their policy perception and job satisfaction predict the intentions. Methods  We conducted a cross-sectional, online survey from December 2021 to February 2022 to investigate GPs’ perception towards NCSP, job satisfaction, and intentions to remain in rural area. Eligible participants were GPs who were required to provide health services as part of NCSP at township health centres of 9 provinces which could represent all NCSP GPs in China. Multinomial logistic regression analyses were performed to explore the associations between policy perceptions, job satisfaction, and intentions to remain. Results  Of 3615 GPs included in the analysis, 442 (12.2%) would like to remain in rural area and 1266 (35.0%) were unsure. Results of the multinomial logistic regression analyses showed that compared with GPs who would leave, GPs with higher perception scores for the restriction on taking postgraduate exam (RRR: 1.93, 95% CI 1.72, 2.16) and the commitment to work for six years (RRR: 1.53, 95% CI 1.31, 1.78) were more likely to remain. In contrast, GPs who had higher perception scores for completing standardised residency training (RRR: 0.75, 95% CI 0.64, 0.88) and passing National Medical Licensing Examinations (RRR: 0.74, 95% CI 0.62, 0.87) were more likely to leave. GPs who were satisfied with the freedom of choosing work methods (RRR: 1.52, 95% CI 1.25, 1.84) and chances of promotion (RRR: 1.60, 95% CI 1.32, 1.94) were more likely to remain. Conclusions  This study highlights the significance of policy perception and job satisfaction on GPs’ intentions to remain in rural area. Factors such as career advancement and the empowerment of GPs to build on and use their skills and abilities should be taken into account when designing rural placement programmes. Keywords  Rural areas, GPs, Retention, Perception towards the policy, Job satisfaction

Background The quantity, quality and distribution of health workforce has been widely recognized as a crucial determinant of health system performance [1]. The availability of a qualified and motivated health workforce contributes to the capacity of health systems to deliver services to the population [2]. However, nearly all countries, particularly rural areas were struggling with the shortage and maldistribution of health workforce that may hamper the progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals and leads to inequalities in health outcomes [3]. In the United States and Canada, only 11.0% or less of physicians provide services in rural areas [4, 5]. The number of physicians per 1000 population in India is about 0.7 for rural communities, in contrast with 1.3 for urban areas [6]. As with other countries, China is confronting with great challenges in the imbalance and inequity in health workforce. In China, the amount of health workforce per 1000 was 1.5 times higher in urban than in rural areas in 2021[7]. As a critical intermediate level of a three-tier rural medical system in China, township health centres (THCs) has played a pivotal role in delivering rural medical care to hundreds of millions of people for more than forty years [8]. However, THCs often face understaffing issues due to the difficulties of recruiting health workforce and employing health workers with high education [9, 10]. In response to the inequalities of healthcare workforce availability between rural and urban areas, the National Development and Reform Commission and five other ministries jointly issued the National Compulsory Service Programme (NCSP) in March 2010 [11]. Twenty two provinces that suffered severe rural physician shortage in central and western China were targeted. Students with rural backgrounds were exclusively recruited and were subsidized to complete the 5-years undergraduate studies [12]. In return, students are obligated to provide rural health service as general practitioners (GPs) in designated THCs for 6 years, during which 3 years were required for the standardised residency training (SRT) [13]. The programme aims to train GPs who have passed the National Medical Licensing Examinations (NMLE) during the service period to meet the demands of health workforce in rural China [14]. In total, almost 60,000 students were recruited under this scheme between 2010 and 2020, and more than 10,000 of them had worked in the designated THCs [15]. Despite the great achievements NCSP has made in recruiting rural health workforce in the past few years, challenges still remain in GPs’ willingness to retain in rural communities [16]. For instance, the study conducted in Shannxi province found that 92.6% of 230 GPs who had enrolled in NCSP (NCSP GPs) expressed their intentions to break the contract after graduating from

the programme [14]. In Xinjiang autonomous region, only 7.8% of 1200 NCSP GPs intended to remain after the compulsory service [17]. By contrast, the proportion of health practitioners who would like to remain after fulfilling the compulsory service was 53.0% in rural Australia [18]and 33.9% in rural Canada [19]. Turnover intention has been a major challenge for THCs in rural China and is associated with a variety of factors such as poor living conditions and infrastructure, and the unsustainable work environment [20]. Job satisfaction, as an indicator of the attitude and feelings an individual has about their work [21], has also been identified as a crucial factor in predicting turnover intention of rural health workforce [20, 22, 23]. While there have been a large body of investigations on turnover intention and job satisfaction among primary health workforce in rural China [20, 24–26], there is a research gap regarding GPs’ perceptions towards NCSP and its potential impact on their turnover intention in rural area. Given the unique role of NCSP GPs, it is necessary to investigate their perceptions towards such policies as the restriction on taking postgraduate exam [16]. Our study sought to examine the impacts of GPs’ perception towards NCSP and job satisfaction on their intentions to remain. Our findings can offer valuable suggestions to increase the retention of GPs in rural area and may provide guidance for other countries embarking on a similar trajectory.

Methods Design, setting, and participants We carried out a cross-sectional study between December 2021 and February 2022 to investigate GPs’ perception towards NCSP, job satisfaction, and intentions to remain in rural area. Based on the number of students enrolled by NCSP, we used stratified random sampling to select 9 provinces out of all the 22 provinces in central and western China where NCSP was implemented. The 9 provinces were Hainan, Hubei, Shanxi, Anhui, Guangxi, Guizhou, Qinghai, Xinjiang and Jilin. To ensure the representativeness and generalizability of the sample, the following criteria were met: (1) the number of GPs from the selected provinces was nearly one third of all NCSP GPs in the 22 provinces; (2) the selected provinces were located in four economic regions of China; (3) the economic development status of the 9 selected provinces measured by GDP could be comparable to that of the other 13 provinces that also implemented NCSP. All in all, our sample could represent all NCSP GPs in China. Details of these information can be found in Additional file 1: Table S1.

Measures Intentions to remain after contract expires The primary outcome of this study was GPs’ intention to remain, evaluated by the question “Will you remain after the contract expires?” Responses included “yes”, “no” and “unsure”.

Socio‑demographic characteristics We asked the participants to specify their gender (male or female), age, place of living before joining NCSP (Urban or Rural), working hours per week (≤ 40, 41–48, 49–54, ≥ 55), monthly net income (≤ 3000, 3001–4000, 4001–5000, > 5000), marital status (married or single), years of service (1, 2, 3, ≥ 4), and presence of children (yes or no).

Perception towards NCSP As is stipulated in the policy, seven items were used to measure GPs’ perceptions towards NCSP. The items were further classified into three categories. The category of Management of exit from the program (MEFP) included restrictions on taking postgraduate exam (MEFP-1), restrictions on changing designated rural settings (MEFP-2), and the commitment to work for six years (MEFP-3). Penalty for breaching the contract (PBC) included the refund of tuition and a payment for the fine (PBC-1), and a record in the integrity management (PBC-2). The other two items in the In-service training (IST) were the completement of SRT (IST-1) and a pass for NMLE (IST-2). The items were developed and issued by the National Development and Reform Commission with the aim of tackling with the shortage of health workforce in rural China [27]. Detailed descriptions of the seven items can be found in Table 1. All the items were measured using a five-point Likert scale (1 = “strongly disagree”, 2 = “disagree”, 3 = “neutral”, 4 = “agree” and 5 = “strongly agree”). Participants who scored higher than 3 were classified into the group of “Agree”. Participants who scored 3 were classified as “neutral”, and participants who scored lower than 3 were in the group of “Disagree”. Cronbach’s alpha of the seven items in our sample was 0.76, considered acceptable in reliability test.

Job satisfaction We used a 10-item Warr-Cook-Wall (WCW) job satisfaction questionnaire to evaluate job satisfaction [32]. The questionnaire measures overall job satisfaction and satisfaction with nine aspects of work (physical work condition, freedom of working methods, colleagues and fellow workers, recognition for work, amount of responsibility, income, opportunity to use abilities, hours of work, and chance of promotion). Each aspect was rated on a fivepoint Likert scale (1 = “very unsatisfied”, 2 = “unsatisfied”,

3 = “neutral”, 4 = “satisfied”, 5 = “very satisfied”). Participants who scored higher than 3 were classified into the group of “Satisfied”. Participants who scored 3 were classified as “neutral”, and participants who scored lower than 3 were in the group of “Dissatisfied”. Cronbach’s alpha in our sample was 0.93.

Data collection All the THCs that had enrolled NCSP GPs within the mandate of provincial-level Health Commissions were informed to encourage their NCSP GPs to participate in the investigation. GPs who were working in the THCs and had been enrolled in NCSP were invited. An internet-based self-administered questionnaire was used for the investigation. The questionnaire was discussed and formulated by experts who already had abundant experience in doing NCSP research. To control the quality of the survey, we added rules to the answering of the survey. For instance, it might be possible that the designated THCs disseminated the survey to GPs who did not enrol in NCSP. We prevented this by asking the question at the beginning of the survey if participants had joined NCSP. If the answer is no, then exit the survey. The question on the province would help us exclude GPs who were not from the selected 9 provinces. Participants who had completed the questionnaire would receive a compensation as return. All participants had been fully informed of the purpose the study.

Statistical analysis Descriptive statistics were used to determine the sociodemographic characteristics of GPs, their perception towards the policy, job satisfaction, and their intentions to remain. Results were presented with frequencies and percentages for categorical variables, and with means and standard variation for continuous variables. Univariate analyses were performed to summarize the socio-demographic characteristics of the sample. Differences in scores of policy perception and job satisfaction among GPs who would remain, leave and were unsure were tested using Chi-Squared test. Multinomial logistic regression was used to determine the associations of policy perception and job satisfaction with GPs’ intentions to remain and unsure relative to those who would leave. Multinomial logistic regression is an extension of binary logistic regression and is appropriate for our three categorical outcome variables [33]. Relative risk ratio (RRR) and confidence intervals were calculated for each independent variable of GPs who would remain and were unsure compared with the reference group, GPs who would leave. Results Sample description In total, 3615 participants completed the survey with a response rate of 50.7% (3615/7135). The participants were NCSP GPs recruited between 2010 and 2013 who had already completed their five years’ undergraduate study, and had or would complete their six years’ obligatory services in the designated THCs at the time

of the investigation. As is shown in Table 2, 52.8% of GPs had no intention to remain after contract expires and 35.0% were unsure. Details of the results by provinces can be found in Additional file 1: Table S2. The mean (SD) age of GPs was 28.3 (2.0) years; 53.1% were female. 90% of the GPs lived in rural area before being enrolled in NCSP. Nearly half of them (47.0%) were married, and 60.0% had children. Over one-third (33.3%) of the GPs worked more than 55 h per week, while only 16.7% of them earned more than 5000 CNY ($746) per month. 37.9% of the GPs served for one year, and 9.9% of them had worked more than four years.

Discussion Based on the large representative sample of NCSP GPs in China, we investigated GPs’ perception towards NCSP and job satisfaction, and identified the factors that were associated with their intentions to remain in rural area. Overall, only 12.2% of GPs expressed an intention to remain. The intention to stay was influenced by GPs’ perceptions towards the policy and job satisfaction. Our findings offered multiple implications for future educational programming and policy schemes to address the shortage of healthcare workforce in rural area. Compared to other items of NCSP, the restriction on taking postgraduate exam had the largest number of GPs who reported a low score of perception. But those with higher scores for the perception of this policy are more likely to remain in rural area. The finding was consistent with another study conducted in Sichuan province, which

also identified pursuing a master’s degree as one of the main reasons for NCSP GPs breaching the contract [34]. In China, the medical master’s degree was conceived as the more established credential than SRT [30]. Physicians with a higher degree are considered to be more competent and may find it easier to secure positions in higherlevel hospitals with higher income [30]. Therefore, GPs who are afraid of their failure in gaining admission to the postgraduate studies may break the contract [35]. Indeed, instead of the restriction on obtaining a master’s degree, it might be easier to encourage NCSP GPs to stay by offering them a more community-based, primary-careoriented postgraduate education [36]. Early and repeated training opportunities in remote communities in the early postgraduate years have been recommended [37]. The education and training curricula could be tailored to fit local contexts [36]. The quality of remote supervision [38]and the exposure to role models during the postgraduate study could also have a positive impact on GPs’ willingness to remain in rural area [39, 40]. In addition, GPs who had a higher score for perception of the completion of six-year obligatory service in rural area were more likely to remain. This is consistent with the result of a medical school in Thailand, in which twothirds of the graduates continued their rural placements after compulsory training [41]. One possible spill-over

Though we cannot identify GPs who did not have the intention to stay in rural area before participating in the programme, the GPs who answered “unsure” suggest the possible existence of this unintended effect. The potential advantages of serving in rural area may inspire the graduates to stay when completing the contract, even if they have not had the intention before participating in NCSP. In addition, GPs who scored higher in the perception of not changing designated rural settings were more likely to remain. The restriction was intended to ensure GPs’ fulfilment of the contract and to meet the urgent needs of human resources posed by the designated THCs in rural China. It is possible that GPs who had a good cognition of the value of rural medical work scored high in not changing the designated rural setting as they were inspired to make their own and long-term contributions to the health of rural residents [14]. Our study found that GPs who had a higher perception score on the record in the integrity management were more likely to remain, compared with those who would leave. The integrity management system for health professionals was established in China in 2013 [28], and was used as additional evidence by health institutions to recruit GPs, evaluate their residency performance and help with the decision on GPs’ postgraduate admissions [29]. For GPs who breach the contract and leave, the record may negatively impact their career development, which, could be one explanation for their lower score on this policy compared with GPs who would remain. Accordingly, as one of the penalties for breaching the contract, the integrity management system might be more feasible in ensuring the effectiveness and sustainability of the programme than paying for the fine, if used in an appropriate way. What’s more, we found that higher scores for completing the SRT and passing the NMLE increases more the risk of GPs leaving rural service compared to the risk of staying. This might be explained by the income differentials between rural and urban practices [42]. GPs who had low valuations of rural life were likely to respond to these income differentials and leave after completing the SRT and passing the NMLE. Their propensity to leave might be even greater if such GPs consider, in addition to wage disparities, postgraduate training restrictions under NCSP and that their demands for career advancement will not be fulfilled in rural service. If so, the clinical knowledge and skills [43] obtained from the SRT and the NMLE will indeed help GPs to leave for more developed urban areas to pursue higher income and better opportunities. In this regard, the completion of SRT and NMLE should not be considered as one of the “incentives” to

increase GPs’ intentions to remain. Instead, completing the 3-year SRT and passing NMLE are simply certification requirements by the Chinese government [44, 45] for all GPs to practice medicine and prescribe medications [46]. The aim of these requirements should be to improve qualified abilities of GPs in rural China [12]. For job satisfaction of GPs in our study, the score of satisfaction with income was the lowest among GPs, followed by the score of chances of promotion. The finding aligned well with another conducted among primary care workforce in China who similarly reported low job satisfaction with income level [47]. A previous study showed that 35.5% of 1133 NCSP GPs thought they would plunge into low-income groups once working in the countryside [48]. Indeed, it was possible for primary care workforce, such as village doctors, to earn more than the net per capita income of local residents [49]. However, when compared with counterparts who earned a higher income in urban areas, village doctors were probably discontented with the status quo and preferred to leave [49]. As is investigated in 2017, the median annual income of doctors with a junior professional title (who typically have 2–10  years of clinical experience after graduating from medical college) in central China was 48,000 CNY ($6969), much higher than it was in village clinics of 25,000 CNY ($3630) [42]. In addition, there was an increasement of GPs’ workload to which three tasks related to public health services were added since 2009 [50, 51]. The increased workload extended GPs’ working hours and might further reduce their income from other part-time jobs [52, 53]. Therefore, in order to retain GPs in rural area, the provision of appropriate financial support such as stipends and subsidies should be taken into account [24, 54]. In particular, the access to and a secure of retirement pension has been found to be an important incentive for health professionals to practice in rural settings [31]. The association between chances of promotion and turnover is consistent with the study of primary care doctors in Chongqing, China, which found that chances of promotion significantly predicted turnover intention [26]. Compared with GPs in other countries who focused on job flexibility [55], such as the chance of working in more than one specialty and labour mobility, GPs in China focused more on job stability and employability [56–58]. This difference could be resulted from the relatively new development of primary care and the unclear career prospects of GPs in China [55, 59]. Providing clear career promotion schemes for GPs could potentially address rural doctor shortages and mitigate the influence of turnover on the provision of health care in rural area [60]. The senior posts in rural healthcare settings can help professionals advance their career ladder through

The non-pecuniary incentives, such as a stable and safe prospect, the achievement in professional field, the fondness for serving others, and an increased proportion of GPs to obtain national honors and prizes for their outstanding performance are the crucial features of GPs in China that should be taken into account when designing strategies for their career development [62]. Of the GPs surveyed, a large proportion reported low scores for hours of work, the physical working conditions, the freedom of working methods, and the opportunity to use abilities. However, the longer hours GPs work, the less likely they would remain. Indeed, GPs had been playing an expanded role in THCs since the integration of public health services with clinical services in 2009 [63]. The mismatch of higher workload and income contribute to GPs’ low job satisfaction, and may further decrease their intentions to remain in rural area [47, 64]. In addition, GPs who scored higher on the satisfaction with physical working conditions were more likely to remain. In a qualitative study of doctors in rural THCs, working conditions were considered as an important factor of job satisfaction [65]. However, 32 out of 39 participants of the study complained about the disorganized situation in THCs, where limited space was available for squeezing into the many kinds of medicines and diagnostic devices [65]. The lack of air conditioning and sanitation workers were other characteristics of the compromised working conditions of rural THCs in China [65]. To improve the overall conditions of THCs, National Health Commission of China had implemented specific standards on the construction of physical working conditions in THCs in 2022, including the construction area, the number of available beds, and the configuration of public devices. The short and long-term effects of this standard on the job satisfaction and turnover intention among GPs in rural THCs can be studied in future research. The freedom of GPs to make rational clinical decisions and to run their practice [66] were the functional dimensions of autonomy [67]. However, the limitation on drug use might contribute to the decreased autonomy of GPs in China [68]. The decreased freedom of medical practice weakened medical service capacity of GPs to some extent [68], and may further make it difficult for GPs to meet the requirements of their job. For work abilities, one study of GPs in Shanghai found that GPs perceived managerial competence, creativity and entrepreneurship important for their careers [62]. These features should then be considered into the design of job opportunities for GPs to meet their demands-abilities fit [69]. Our study has several limitations. First, the causal interpretation of our results was limited due to the

cross-sectional nature of the study. A well conducted, purpose built, ongoing study is recommended to produce robust evidence on the long-term or dynamic effect of perceptions towards the policy and job satisfaction on GPs’ career choice [70]. Second, the survey dataset used in our study is subjected to well-known self-reported bias. For instance, the extent to which rural background predisposes medical students to become rural doctors would be dependent upon some environmental factors about the area [71]. That’s why survey participants might say they are interested in rural or public health service but intentions do not always play out in real-life. Third, additional factors, such as family support and an optimism toward THC development [72] should be identified in future research through in-depth interviews with relevant stakeholders. Fourth, to better modulate the response intensity, a standardized scale such as a 1 to 5 rating system could be used to gauge the intention of stay or leave in the future research. Fifth, considering the contextual differences between provinces, characteristics of rural territories such as the residing populations, the regions’ sizes, the level of urbanization, the capacity of the local primary care service, and the remuneration and payment system should be taken into account in future research to study GPs’ turnover intention.

Conclusions The significant associations between GPs’ perceptions towards NCSP, job satisfaction and their intentions to remain suggest important features of GPs for policymakers to take into account when recruiting and retaining rural medical students. Rural healthcare institutions may consider strengthening career advancement of GPs and empowering GPs to build on and use their skills and competencies with the appropriate freedom of choosing their own working methods. Because of the shortage of healthcare workforce in rural area, evidence-based strategies for improving retention in general practice at the primary health care level are needed in China and likely in other settings.

# Work stress and competency among radiology residents: the mediating effect of resilience

1 Vanke School of Public Health, Tsinghua University, Beijing, China, 2 School of Medicine, Tsinghua University, Beijing, China, 3 National Centre for Health Professions Education Development, Graduate School of Education, Peking University, Beijing, China, 4 Shengzhou High School, ZheJiang, China,

5 Department of Radiology, Beijing Friendship Hospital, Capital Medical University, Beijing, China,

6 Department of Radiology, Ningbo No. 2 Hospital, Ningbo, China, 7 Institute for Healthy China, Tsinghua University, Beijing, China

Background: Competency of health professionals stands as a fundamental element in ensuring the quality of care. Notably, work stress and resilience are found to be associated with competency of health professionals. However, the role of resilience between work stress and competency remains unexplored. This study aims to investigate competency, work stress and resilience of radiology residents, and to examine the mediating effect of resilience.

Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 3,666 radiology residents from 31 provinces of China in 2021. The diagnostic radiology milestones were used to measure the competency. Results of work stress and resilience were derived from self-reports and assessment of the Connor Davidson Resilience Scale (CD-RISC) respectively. To examine the association between work stress, resilience, and competency, Spearman correlation analysis and hierarchical linear regression were employed. The mediating effect of resilience was tested by bootstrapping analysis.

Results: Descriptive statistics show that the average score (mean  ±  SD) of work stress, competency and resilience among radiology residents were 1.55 ± 1.53 (range from 0 to 6), 28.14  ±  13 (range from 0 to 81) and 5.97  ±  1.92 (range from 0 to 8), respectively. Work stress was negatively associated with competency (β  = −0.51, p  <  0.001) and resilience (−0.57, p  <  0.001). In particular, resilience mediated the relationship between work stress and competence, and the total mediating effect was −0.49 (= −  0.57 * 0.86), accounting for 49.06% of the total effect.

Conclusion: Work stress is a significant contributor to competence among radiology residents. Resilience significantly mediated the association. This study highlights incorporating resilience training courses into the standardized residency training program to reduce intensive work stress and promote competency of radiology residents.
